RAG DATASET: COLLECTION &
PREPARATION
Practical class notes for the Academic Question Answering System
Purpose: help you decide what data to collect, where to get it, how to organize it, and how to prepare
it for a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) project.
This guide helps you answer
What you should produce
Which documents should I collect?
A source list and approved document folder
How should I organize them?
A consistent metadata sheet
How do I prepare documents for RAG?
Clean text, chunks, and source locations
How do I test the project?
A separate evaluation question set
Recommended beginner scope: Start with one subject or a small set of subjects, use trusted course materials, and expand
only after the first end-to-end tests work.

1. What Does “Dataset” Mean in a RAG Project?
In machine learning, “dataset” often means a collection of examples used to train or evaluate a model. In a RAG system, the
main dataset is usually a knowledge collection: documents the system searches at question time. RAG normally retrieves
these documents; it does not require training a new language model on them.
You should plan for three related data collections
Collection
Contains
Main use
A. Knowledge documents
Syllabus, lecture notes, textbooks or open
resources, lab manuals, official FAQs.
Provides evidence for answers.
B. Source metadata
Title, subject, unit, page, version, origin,
permissions.
Makes search filters and citations possible.
C. Evaluation dataset
Test questions, expected key points, expected
sources, review scores.
Measures whether retrieval, answers, and
citations work.
For your project, keep the knowledge documents and evaluation dataset separate. Do not use only a list of question-answer
pairs as the knowledge base if the goal is to answer questions from full academic notes.

Suggested collection for a first prototype
• One current syllabus for the selected subject.
• Five to fifteen useful lecture-note or study-note files, if available and permitted.
• Relevant lab/manual material only if your system will answer practical questions.
• A small collection of PYQs for evaluation or coverage analysis.
• A separate set of questions written by you and checked against the notes.
These quantities are a manageable starting point, not a universal requirement. Quality, readable text, and traceable sources
matter more than collecting a huge number of files immediately.
3. Where Can You Get the Data?
• Your course: official syllabus, faculty-provided notes, lab manuals, and permitted assignments.
• Your own material: notes you wrote yourself, after checking accuracy.
• Open educational resources: resources whose license allows your intended use; record the license and attribution.
• Official documentation: suitable when the project covers tools or technologies and those sources are relevant.
• Past exam papers: only from authorized or publicly available sources, and only if institutional rules permit their use.

Avoid collecting random internet PDFs without checking their source, accuracy, version, and permissions. Do not include
private student records, answer sheets with personal details, or restricted exam material without authorization.
4. Make a Document Inventory
Before processing files, create a spreadsheet called document_inventory. Give each file a stable ID and record where it
came from. This inventory becomes the source of truth for your project.

Simple file organization
Keep a clean folder structure, for example: dataset/original_documents/, dataset/processed_text/, dataset/metadata/, and
dataset/evaluation/. Keep originals unchanged so you can trace a processed passage back to its source.
5. Check and Clean Your Documents
• Confirm that each file opens and is readable.
• Check whether the PDF contains selectable text or only scanned page images.
• For scanned files, OCR may be needed; inspect the output manually.
• Preserve headings, page boundaries, tables, formulas, and numbered steps when they matter.

• Check whether the PDF contains selectable text or only scanned page images.
• For scanned files, OCR may be needed; inspect the output manually.
• Preserve headings, page boundaries, tables, formulas, and numbered steps when they matter.
• Remove repeated headers/footers only if doing so will not remove meaningful information.
• Mark duplicate files and choose the intended version.
• Check that extraction has not changed symbols such as ≤, ≥, subscripts, equations, or code snippets.
• Keep a record of files excluded and the reason for excluding them.
Do not silently “correct” academic content during cleaning. If a source appears to contain an error, flag it for review or keep the
source faithful and record the issue.
6. Chunk-Level Dataset and Metadata
After extracting text, divide each document into chunks—small passages that can be retrieved independently. A chunk should
usually focus on one coherent idea while keeping enough context to understand it.
Chunk field
Purpose
chunk_id
Unique ID for this passage.
document_id
Connects the chunk to the original inventory record.
chunk_text
The actual text passage used for retrieval and context.
subject / unit / section
Supports filtering and understandable citations.
page_start / page_end
Lets users find the passage in the original file.

Chunk field
Purpose
chunk_index
Records the chunk's order within the document.
document_version
Helps prevent citations to outdated material.
How to decide chunk size
There is no single correct chunk size for every dataset. Start with headings and paragraphs as natural boundaries, keep
related explanation together, and test whether your retrieval results contain enough context. Overlap neighboring chunks a little
if splitting would otherwise break a definition from its explanation.
Important distinction
The original document is the source. Extracted text and chunks are processed representations of that source. Preserve the
mapping from each chunk back to its document and page or section; otherwise, citations become difficult to trust.
7. Build a Separate Evaluation Dataset
Your evaluation dataset is a set of questions used to test the system. Each question should have a reference answer or key
points and the source passages that support them.
Field
Example
question_id
Q_DBMS_001
question

question_type
Definition / explanation
expected_key_points
Purpose of normalization; reduction of redundancy; relevant caveat if covered.
expected_document_id
DBMS_NOTE_001
expected_page_or_section

difficulty

answerable_from_dataset

review_status

Include several question types
• Definition: “What is a primary key?”
• Explanation: “Explain normalization in simple terms.”
• Comparison: “Differentiate a process and a thread.”
• Multi-part: “List and explain the ACID properties.”
• Exact lookup: “Which topics are in Unit 3?”
• Paraphrased: ask the same concept using different wording.
• Out-of-scope: ask about a topic that is not in the collection.
• Ambiguous or conflicting: check whether the system asks for clarification or identifies conflicting sources.

• Out-of-scope: ask about a topic that is not in the collection.
• Ambiguous or conflicting: check whether the system asks for clarification or identifies conflicting sources.
Keep some test questions aside until development is complete. If you repeatedly tune the system using every test question, the
final evaluation may overstate performance.

9. Sample Dataset Plan for a College Project
Example scope: a prototype for one subject, such as DBMS or Operating Systems. The exact subject should match the
materials you can legitimately access.
Dataset item
Initial plan

Lecture/study notes
A small curated set

Lab/manual files
Only if practical questions are in scope

PYQs

Evaluation questions
A varied set written and source-checked by you

Several questions absent from the collection
Checks whether the system avoids guessing.
Do not claim a particular dataset size is sufficient without testing. Start small, check retrieval and citation quality, and add
documents based on observed coverage gaps.
10. Ready-to-Use Dataset Checklist

Several questions absent from the collection
Checks whether the system avoids guessing.
Do not claim a particular dataset size is sufficient without testing. Start small, check retrieval and citation quality, and add
documents based on observed coverage gaps.
10. Ready-to-Use Dataset Checklist
• I have defined the subject(s) and the kinds of questions the system should answer.
• Every document has a stable ID and a recorded source.
• I have checked accuracy, version, readability, and permissions.
• Original files are preserved separately from processed text.
• Each chunk stores its document ID and page/section metadata.
• I have checked extracted text for broken formulas, tables, and headings.
• My evaluation questions have reference key points and source locations.
• Some test questions are kept separate from development examples.
• I have questions with missing evidence to test abstention.
• I can trace any displayed citation back to the original source.
11. What to Explain in Your Report
Describe the dataset sources and why they were selected, the subjects and topic coverage, the number and types of
documents actually collected, the cleaning and extraction process, the chunking strategy, the metadata fields, and how the
evaluation questions were prepared. Report the real counts after collection—do not invent numbers in advance.
Example methodology wording: “The knowledge collection was built from approved academic materials. Each document was
assigned a unique identifier and metadata describing its subject, unit, version, and source. Text was extracted and reviewed,

then divided into passages while preserving source locations. A separate evaluation set was created with questions, expected
key points, and supporting source references.”
